title: Lexical Analysis
summary: Turning raw characters into a token stream — the first, and simplest, stage of the pipeline. Regular expressions and DFAs are the whole mechanism, and "maximal munch" is the one rule that resolves most of the ambiguity.

slides.markdown:
Lexical analysis is the pipeline's first stage: turn a flat stream of characters into a flat stream of **tokens** — the atomic units a parser can reason about, like `IDENT(x)`, `NUM(2)`, `PLUS`, without any structure between them yet.

The lexer's whole job description fits in one sentence: recognize the longest valid token starting at the current position, emit it, and move on. That's it — no nesting, no recursion, no grammar. The theory behind it (regular expressions, finite automata) is exactly the theory behind `grep` and `.gitignore` patterns; a lexer is a regex engine applied to source code, one token at a time.

What trips people up isn't the theory — it's a handful of real edge cases (`<=` vs `<` then `=`, keywords vs identifiers, comments) that every working lexer has to get right, covered here.

A **token** pairs a category with, usually, the actual text it matched: `IDENT("total")`, `NUM("42")`, `KEYWORD("if")`, `PLUS`, `LPAREN`. The categories that matter across almost every language: keywords (`if`, `return`), identifiers (variable/function names), literals (numbers, strings, booleans), operators (`+`, `==`), and punctuation (`(`, `;`, `{`).

The token stream throws away information the parser doesn't need at this stage — exact whitespace, exact column position (mostly kept only for error messages), comments — and keeps exactly what's needed to build structure next. `x  =  1+2;` and `x=1+2;` produce the identical token stream; the lexer has already normalized away the formatting differences a human cares about but a parser doesn't.

Each token category is defined by a regular expression: an identifier might be `[a-zA-Z_][a-zA-Z0-9_]*`, an integer literal `[0-9]+`, a keyword a fixed literal string. The lexer's generator-level job is just: given the current position in the source, which of these patterns matches the longest prefix, and which category does it belong to.

This is why lexical analysis is theoretically simple compared to parsing: regular languages (what regexes describe) are strictly less expressive than context-free languages (what grammars describe) — a regex fundamentally can't count or nest, which is exactly why balanced parentheses need a parser, not a lexer. Token recognition doesn't need that power; it's genuinely a regular-language problem end to end.

![DFA state machine scanning identifier and number tokens character by character](assets/lexer-dfa.svg)

Each regex compiles to an NFA, and NFAs get converted to an equivalent DFA for actual execution, because a DFA has exactly one active state at a time — no branching, no backtracking — making per-character scanning a simple table lookup. This is the same automaton theory that powers `grep`, just wired up to emit tokens instead of match/no-match.

slides.subTitle: Why `<=` isn't `<` then `=`
slides.markdown:
**Maximal munch**: at each position, the lexer takes the *longest* possible match, not the first one that happens to work. Scanning `<=`, a lexer that greedily tried the shortest match first would tokenize `<` as `LT`, then separately match `=` as `ASSIGN` — two tokens, wrong result. Maximal munch says: check if a longer match starting here is possible (`<=` as one `LE` token) before settling for a shorter one, and take the longer one when it's valid.

This is why lexer specifications for languages with multi-character operators always order or structure their rules so the longest applicable token wins — `<=`, `==`, `->`, `**` all depend on this rule to be recognized as single tokens instead of accidentally splitting into two shorter, individually-valid ones.

Whitespace and comments are matched by the lexer like anything else, but they're almost always **discarded** rather than turned into tokens — the parser's grammar has no rule that expects a comment token to appear between an `if` and its condition, so keeping them would force every grammar rule to account for optional noise everywhere. (Some lexers do keep them as attached trivia for tools that need exact source text back — formatters, IDEs — but the parser itself never sees them.)

A **lexical error** happens when no rule matches at the current position at all — an invalid character, an unterminated string literal that runs off the end of the file. This is the earliest point a source file can fail, and the error message it produces ("unexpected character") is the most specific, localized kind of compiler error there is, precisely because the lexer hasn't tried to understand anything about structure or meaning yet.

`if`, `return`, and `total` are all lexically identical patterns — `[a-zA-Z_][a-zA-Z0-9_]*` matches every one of them. Writing a separate regex per keyword to distinguish them from identifiers works but scales badly and gets ambiguous fast as the keyword list grows.

The standard fix: lex *everything* matching the identifier pattern as `IDENT` first, then look the matched text up in a fixed **keyword table**. If it's there, re-tag the token as the specific keyword (`IF`, `RETURN`); if not, it's a genuine identifier. This is why `if` can't be used as a variable name in most languages — the keyword table check happens unconditionally on every identifier-shaped token, with no way to opt out — and why some languages carve out **contextual keywords** (words that are keywords only in specific positions) as a deliberate, more complex exception to this simple table lookup.

slides.sectionTitle: Write a tokenizer for a calculator
slides.markdown:
This is a live-coding staple precisely because it's small enough to finish in the time given and still tests the real mechanics: a position cursor, per-character-class branching, and multi-character lookahead for anything longer than one character.

A solid walkthrough for `12 + 34 * (5 - 6)`: skip whitespace unconditionally; on a digit, greedily consume every following digit into one `NUM` token (not one token per digit — a classic first-attempt bug); on `+ - * / ( )`, emit a single-character operator token directly; on anything else, raise a clear lexical error naming the offending character and position. Mentioning maximal munch explicitly — even though this grammar has no multi-character operators to trigger it — signals you know the general rule, not just this specific case.

slides.sectionTitle: What lexing hands off to parsing
slides.markdown:
The lexer's output contract is simple and strict: a flat sequence of tokens, each with a category and the matched text, in source order, with whitespace and comments already stripped out. That flatness is exactly what [parsing-and-grammars](parsing-and-grammars) needs as its input — a parser reasons about *structure between tokens*, and it can only do that cleanly if the tokens themselves are already unambiguous, atomic units.

Everything genuinely hard about turning source into a program — precedence, nesting, matching a `return` to its enclosing function — is deliberately *not* the lexer's problem. That's the next stage's job, and it's a strictly more powerful kind of analysis for exactly that reason.
